chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, altogether from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the hunted prey which the man shoots at with an arrow, and it hits it sideways and kills it, and he had invoked the Name (Bismillah) when he shot it, but the iron (arrowhead) did not hit it.
So he (peace be upon him) said: If it was the arrow which struck it that also killed it, then when he sees it as such, let him eat.

key_terms.الحديدة: The iron; refers specifically to the arrowhead or cutting/piercing edge. Its contact with the prey is normally required for permissibility.
key_terms.الصيد: Hunted prey; the object of lawful hunting. Islamic jurisprudence carefully regulates the conditions under which hunted animal flesh is permissible.
key_terms.سمّى: Invoked the Name (of God); the requirement to say 'Bismillah' (In the name of God) at the moment of releasing the weapon is a prerequisite for the permissibility of the kill.
key_terms.معترضاً: Sideways/crosswise; describes the prey being hit by the shaft of the arrow rather than by the metal tip.

ai.seo_question: Is hunting permissible if the arrow hits prey sideways without the arrowhead making contact according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Al-Halabi asked Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) about an unusual hunting scenario: an arrow strikes prey sideways (with the shaft rather than the arrowhead) and kills it, though the hunter had pronounced 'Bismillah' at the time of release. The Imam ruled that if the same arrow that struck the prey is confirmed to be what caused its death, the meat is permissible to eat. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that the decisive factor in the permissibility of hunted meat is the actual cause of death from the shot arrow, combined with the proper invocation of God's name at the moment of release.
